name: Dawn of agriculture
summary: Farming was invented independently in several regions, beginning with the Fertile Crescent, and permanently changed how humans live.
body:
Wheat, barley, peas, sheep and goats were domesticated in the hills of the Levant and upper Mesopotamia; rice in the Yangtze valley, maize in Mexico, potatoes in the Andes.

Food surpluses allowed permanent villages, storable wealth, specialists and eventually cities — but also poorer diets, epidemic disease and hierarchy. Everything from [writing](event:writing) to the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution) rests on this foundation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution).

name: Göbekli Tepe
summary: Hunter-gatherers raised monumental carved pillars in southeastern Anatolia, before pottery or farming villages.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). Circles of T-shaped limestone pillars up to 5.5 m tall are decorated with foxes, snakes and vultures. The site suggests that large-scale ritual gathering may have preceded, rather than followed, settled agriculture.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Göbekli_Tepe).

name: Walls of Jericho
summary: One of the world's oldest continuously occupied settlements built a stone wall and tower.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). One of the world's oldest continuously occupied settlements built a stone wall and tower.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jericho).

name: Domestication of livestock
summary: Sheep, goats, pigs and cattle were brought under human management, followed later by the horse.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). Domestic animals supplied meat, milk, wool, traction and manure — and, in close quarters, the zoonotic diseases that would later devastate populations without immunity.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestication_of_animals).

name: Çatalhöyük
summary: A dense Neolithic town in Anatolia housing several thousand people in mudbrick houses entered through the roof.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). A dense Neolithic town in Anatolia housing several thousand people in mudbrick houses entered through the roof.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Çatalhöyük).

name: Rise of Uruk and the first cities
summary: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia grew into arguably the world's first city, with tens of thousands of inhabitants.
body:
Monumental temples, mass-produced pottery and administrative seals mark the emergence of a state-scale society, and the accounting needs of its temples produced [writing](event:writing).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruk).

name: Invention of the wheel
summary: Potters' wheels and then wheeled vehicles appeared across Mesopotamia and the Pontic steppe.
body:
The oldest wheeled-vehicle images and surviving wheels date to the fourth millennium BCE; the axle, not the wheel itself, was the hard part.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheel).

name: Bronze Age begins
summary: Alloying copper with tin produced a metal hard enough for tools and weapons, and trade networks to carry the ingredients.
body:
Tin is rare and rarely found near copper, so bronze required long-distance exchange stretching from Cornwall and Afghanistan to the Mediterranean — a fragility that helped bring on the [Late Bronze Age collapse](event:bronze-age-collapse).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age).

name: Invention of writing
summary: Cuneiform accounting marks in Sumer became the first true writing system, with Egyptian hieroglyphs following within a century or two.
body:
What began as tokens for counting grain and livestock became, within a few centuries, a full script able to record law, literature and history — and with it the first records that historians can read directly.

Writing was invented independently at least three more times: in China, in Mesoamerica, and probably in the Indus valley.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_writing).

name: Unification of Egypt
summary: Upper and Lower Egypt were unified under a single king, traditionally Narmer, beginning three millennia of pharaonic civilisation.
body:
The Narmer Palette shows the king wearing the crowns of both lands. The state that emerged, bound together by the Nile, outlasted every one of its Bronze Age contemporaries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Dynastic_Period_(Egypt)).

name: Minoan civilization of Crete
summary: A seafaring Bronze Age culture on Crete built palaces, a merchant fleet and an undeciphered script.
body:
Knossos, the largest palace, contained plumbing, frescoes and storage for hundreds of olive oil jars. The Minoans traded across the Mediterranean and wrote in a still undeciphered script, Linear A. The [Thera eruption](event:thera-eruption) struck the southern Aegean around 1600 BCE, and by about 1450 BCE the palaces had passed into Mycenaean hands.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_civilization).

name: Indus Valley civilisation
summary: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa held grid-planned cities with drains, standardised bricks and a script still undeciphered.
body:
At its height the civilisation covered a larger area than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined, apparently without palaces, royal tombs or obvious armies.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_Valley_Civilisation).

name: Stonehenge
summary: The sarsen circle was raised on Salisbury Plain, aligned on the solstice sunrise and sunset.
body:
The bluestones were dragged or carried some 250 km from the Preseli hills of Wales.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge).

name: Great Pyramid of Giza
summary: Khufu's tomb, 146 metres tall and built from over two million blocks, was the tallest structure on Earth for 3,800 years.
body:
Part of [Unification of Egypt](event:egypt-unification). It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing, and was raised by a paid, organised workforce rather than by slaves.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza).

name: Akkadian Empire
summary: Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian cities and assembled what is often called the first empire.
body:
It ran on standing armies, appointed governors and a common language of administration — a template later empires would recognise. Drought may have brought it down.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akkadian_Empire).

name: Code of Ur-Nammu
summary: The oldest surviving law code predates Hammurabi by about three centuries, setting out written justice in Sumer.
body:
Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur, or his son Shulgi, had the laws set down in Sumerian; they survive in later clay-tablet copies covering theft, injury and negligent building. Far shorter than the [Code of Hammurabi](event:hammurabi) but three centuries older, it shows written law already emerging across Mesopotamia.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Ur-Nammu).

name: Egypt's Middle Kingdom
summary: A golden age of Egyptian art, literature and stable governance, when the state reasserted control after the First Intermediate Period.
body:
Pharaohs like Amenemhat III brought Egypt together again after fragmentation. The era saw flourishing literature, refined sculpture and architecture, and the height of Egyptian bureaucratic sophistication.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Kingdom_of_Egypt).

name: Code of Hammurabi
summary: The Babylonian king had 282 laws carved on a basalt stele and set up in public.
body:
It is not the earliest law code, but it is the most complete, and it fixed the principle that the law was written down and knowable rather than the king's whim of the day.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi).

name: Rise of the Hittite Empire
summary: The Hittites of Anatolia built an empire that rivalled Egypt and fought Ramesses II to a standstill at Kadesh.
body:
From their capital at Hattusa they assembled a state of vassal kingdoms, a chariot army and detailed law codes, and fought Egypt at [Kadesh](event:kadesh) before agreeing one of the first recorded peace treaties. The empire fell apart in the [Late Bronze Age collapse](event:bronze-age-collapse).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hittites).

name: Eruption of Thera
summary: One of the largest eruptions of the Holocene destroyed the Minoan town of Akrotiri on Santorini.
body:
Ash and tsunamis struck Crete, and the buried town — preserved like a Bronze Age Pompeii — has been linked, speculatively, to the legend of Atlantis.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_eruption).

name: Mycenaean civilization
summary: Mainland Greek palace kingdoms built citadels, traded across the Mediterranean and left the first written Greek.
body:
Palace centres like Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos were run by warrior kings and kept their accounts in Linear B, the earliest written form of Greek. Later Greeks remembered this age in the legends of the [Trojan War](event:trojan-war); the palaces burned during the [Late Bronze Age collapse](event:bronze-age-collapse).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece).

name: Shang dynasty
summary: The first Chinese dynasty attested by contemporary writing, ruling from Anyang with bronze ritual vessels and oracle bones.
body:
Questions inscribed on ox scapulae and turtle plastrons are the ancestors of the Chinese script still in use today.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty).

name: Vedic period in India
summary: The Vedas were composed in Sanskrit, laying the foundations of Hindu religion, ritual and social order.
body:
The Vedas were composed in Sanskrit, laying the foundations of Hindu religion, ritual and social order.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_period).

name: Battle of Kadesh
summary: Egyptians under Ramesses II fought the Hittites to a draw; the peace that followed is the earliest surviving international treaty.
body:
Egyptians under Ramesses II fought the Hittites to a draw; the peace that followed is the earliest surviving international treaty.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kadesh).

name: Iron Age begins
summary: Ironworking spread from Anatolia across Eurasia and Africa, putting hard metal within reach of ordinary farmers and soldiers.
body:
Unlike bronze, iron ore is common almost everywhere, so the new metal broke the trade dependency that had constrained the [Bronze Age](event:bronze-age).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age).

name: Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: Within about fifty years the Hittite empire, Mycenaean Greece and the great trading cities of the Levant were all destroyed or abandoned.
body:
Ugarit, Hattusa and Pylos burned; Egypt survived but was permanently weakened after fighting off the "Sea Peoples". Drought, earthquake swarms, migration and the collapse of interlocking trade networks all seem to be involved.

Greece lost writing altogether for four centuries — a genuine dark age.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Bronze_Age_collapse).

name: Chinese oracle bone divination
summary: Ox scapulae and turtle shells inscribed for divination by the Shang carry the earliest known Chinese writing.
body:
Part of [Shang dynasty](event:shang-dynasty). Diviners applied heat to the bones, read the cracks, and inscribed the question and the outcome beside them. These inscriptions are the first direct evidence of the Chinese language and of what the Shang court worried about.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_bone_script).

name: Trojan War
summary: The legendary siege of Troy, dated by later Greeks to the twelfth century BCE and immortalised in the *Iliad*.
body:
Part of [Late Bronze Age collapse](event:bronze-age-collapse). The legendary siege of Troy, dated by later Greeks to the twelfth century BCE and immortalised in the *Iliad*.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_War).

name: Kingdom of Kush rises in Nubia
summary: A Nubian kingdom on the upper Nile rivalled Egypt, ruled it as the 25th Dynasty, and built hundreds of steep pyramids of its own.
body:
Kush emerged around Napata as Egyptian power waned, and its kings ruled Egypt itself for a century. The capital later moved south to Meroe, a centre of iron working and of trade in gold, incense and ivory reaching from inner Africa to the Mediterranean.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Kush).

name: Phoenician alphabet
summary: A script of about 22 consonant signs, simple enough for merchants to learn, spread around the Mediterranean.
body:
Greek, Latin, Aramaic, Hebrew and Arabic all descend from it, as does — through Latin — the alphabet you are reading now.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet).

name: Zhou Dynasty
summary: China's longest dynasty saw the invention of the 'Mandate of Heaven', feudal government and the philosophical flowering of the Axial Age.
body:
The Zhou overthrew the [Shang](event:shang-dynasty), claiming that heaven had withdrawn its mandate from a failed ruler. Their system of regional lords foreshadowed later imperial administration, and the disorder of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods produced [Confucius](event:confucius), Laozi and the other classical Chinese thinkers.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_dynasty).

name: Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem
summary: The First Temple was built in Jerusalem, becoming the centre of Israelite worship until its destruction in 587 BCE.
body:
The First Temple was built in Jerusalem, becoming the centre of Israelite worship until its destruction in 587 BCE.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon%27s_Temple).

name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
summary: Assyria built the largest empire the world had yet seen, ruling from Nineveh with siege engines, mass deportation and a road system.
body:
Assyria built the largest empire the world had yet seen, ruling from Nineveh with siege engines, mass deportation and a road system.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Assyrian_Empire).

name: Founding of Carthage
summary: Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded the city that would dominate the western Mediterranean until the [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars).
body:
Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded the city that would dominate the western Mediterranean until the [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage).

name: Greek alphabet emerges
summary: Greeks adapted the Phoenician script, added signs for vowels, and produced the ancestor of the Western alphabets.
body:
Part of [Phoenician alphabet](event:phoenician-alphabet). Writing vowels as well as consonants made the Greek script phonetically complete and easy to learn. Writing spread beyond a narrow scribal class over the following centuries, though full literacy remained limited.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_alphabet).

name: First Olympic Games
summary: The traditional date of the first games at Olympia, which the Greeks used as the origin of their shared chronology.
body:
The traditional date of the first games at Olympia, which the Greeks used as the origin of their shared chronology.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Olympic_Games).

name: Founding of Rome
summary: Traditional date of Rome's founding, the seed of the republic and empire that would shape the Mediterranean world.
body:
Archaeology shows settlement on the Palatine from at least the tenth century BCE; the Romulus legend gave the city a founding myth to match its later power.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_of_Rome).

name: Etruscan civilisation influences Rome
summary: The Etruscans of central Italy shaped early Roman religion, government, architecture and culture.
body:
From the Etruscans Rome took augury (reading omens in the flight of birds) and haruspicy (inspecting the livers of sacrificed animals), temple design, drainage engineering and, by way of Greek traders, the alphabet. Etruscan kings ruled Rome until the Republic, and Etruscan practice shaped Roman religion long after.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etruscan_civilization).

name: Early Greek philosophers
summary: Thales, Pythagoras, Heraclitus and others sought natural explanations for the world rather than mythological ones.
body:
Thales was credited by later Greeks with predicting an eclipse and held that the Earth floats on water; Pythagoras found ratios linking music and number; Heraclitus declared that all things flow. They worked in the Greek cities of Ionia and southern Italy rather than in Athens.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presocratic_philosophy).

name: Zoroastrianism in Persia
summary: An ancient Persian faith, dualist in outlook, whose ideas of a final judgment are often argued to have influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
body:
Zoroaster taught of a cosmic struggle between truth and falsehood, resolved by a final judgment. His own dates are uncertain, with estimates ranging from about 1500 to 600 BCE. The [Achaemenid Empire](event:achaemenid-empire) invoked the god Ahura Mazda, and Zoroastrianism was the state religion of the later Sasanian empire until the Arab conquest.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoroastrianism).

name: Life of the Buddha
summary: Siddhartha Gautama taught in the Ganges plain, founding one of the world's great religious and philosophical traditions.
body:
His teaching — the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path — spread with merchants and, later, with the patronage of [Ashoka](event:maurya-empire) across South, Central and East Asia.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gautama_Buddha).

name: Confucius
summary: Kong Qiu taught an ethic of duty, ritual propriety and learning that shaped Chinese government and society for two millennia.
body:
Confucian texts became the syllabus of the imperial examinations, making his thought the working philosophy of the Chinese state from the [Han](event:han-dynasty) onward.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confucius).

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
summary: Cyrus the Great and his successors ruled from the Aegean to the Indus, the largest empire the world had seen.
body:
The Persians governed through satrapies, a royal road, a standardised coinage and a policy of religious tolerance — Cyrus is remembered in the Hebrew Bible for allowing the Judean exiles to return.

It fell to [Alexander](event:alexander-conquests) in 330 BCE.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire).

name: Roman Republic formally established
summary: Rome replaced its kings with elected magistrates and citizen assemblies, a constitution that lasted nearly five centuries.
body:
Tradition dates the expulsion of the last king to 509 BCE; historians see a slower shift away from monarchy. What emerged was a balance of the Senate, annually elected consuls and popular assemblies — a template later republics would study and imitate.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic).

name: Athenian democracy
summary: The reforms of Cleisthenes gave political power to the assembly of citizens, inventing direct democracy.
body:
Roughly 30,000 adult male citizens could vote; women, resident foreigners and a very large enslaved population could not. Even so, the idea that ordinary people should decide public matters begins here.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian_democracy).

name: Hinduism takes classical form
summary: The Vedas, Upanishads and Puranas crystallise the cosmology, deities and rituals of Hinduism over a millennium.
body:
The [Vedic period](event:vedic-period) produced the foundation hymns; the Upanishads added philosophical enquiry; the epics and Puranas supplied mythology and devotional worship. By the early centuries CE the framework of dharma, karma and rebirth was well established.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism).

name: Hebrew Bible canon formed
summary: Jewish scholars collected and standardised the Torah, Prophets and Writings, settling a canon that later communities preserved.
body:
After the Babylonian exile, Jewish communities gathered, edited and copied the texts that had held them together. The resulting scriptures became the foundation of Judaism, were carried into Christianity as the Old Testament, and shaped Islamic tradition in turn.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_Bible).

name: Iron working spreads in sub-Saharan Africa
summary: Smelting furnaces appear across sub-Saharan Africa, from the Nok culture of Nigeria to the Great Lakes, reshaping farming and trade.
body:
Whether the technique was invented locally or carried across the Sahara is still argued. Iron hoes and axes made heavy soils and woodland workable, and ironworking spread alongside the long Bantu migrations that reshaped the languages of central and southern Africa.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_metallurgy_in_Africa).

name: Greco-Persian Wars
summary: The Greek city-states repelled two Persian invasions, a victory that shaped Greek self-understanding for centuries.
body:
The wars produced [Marathon](event:marathon), [Thermopylae](event:thermopylae) and [Salamis](event:salamis), and their telling by Herodotus effectively invented history as a literary form.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Persian_Wars).

name: Battle of Marathon
summary: An outnumbered Athenian hoplite army defeated the Persian landing force on the plain of Marathon.
body:
Part of [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars). An outnumbered Athenian hoplite army defeated the Persian landing force on the plain of Marathon.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon).

name: Battle of Thermopylae
summary: Leonidas and a small Greek force held the coastal pass for three days against Xerxes' army before being outflanked.
body:
Part of [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars). Leonidas and a small Greek force held the coastal pass for three days against Xerxes' army before being outflanked.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Thermopylae).

name: Battle of Salamis
summary: The Greek fleet destroyed the larger Persian navy in the narrows off Salamis, forcing Xerxes to withdraw.
body:
Part of [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars). The Greek fleet destroyed the larger Persian navy in the narrows off Salamis, forcing Xerxes to withdraw.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Salamis).

name: Roman law developed and codified
summary: A system of jurisprudence emerged over centuries, from the Twelve Tables to Justinian's Digest, shaping all later Western law.
body:
Roman law separated public from private law and worked out concepts of legal personality, contract, inheritance and property. [Justinian's](event:justinian) jurists compiled it in the sixth century; medieval universities revived it; and modern civil law systems across Europe, Latin America and Asia descend from it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_law).

name: Parthenon built
summary: Athens crowned its Acropolis with a marble temple to Athena, paid for out of the tribute of its empire.
body:
Part of [Athenian democracy](event:athenian-democracy). Athens crowned its Acropolis with a marble temple to Athena, paid for out of the tribute of its empire.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon).

name: Herodotus writes the Histories
summary: The "Father of History" wrote the first extended prose enquiry into the past, centred on the Greco-Persian Wars.
body:
Herodotus travelled widely through the Persian empire and the eastern Mediterranean, collecting stories and questioning witnesses. His account of the [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars) mixes reporting, hearsay and legend, but it established the idea that the past should be investigated and written as a connected narrative.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herodotus).

name: Peloponnesian War
summary: Athens and Sparta fought for 27 years; Athens lost its fleet, its empire and, for a time, its democracy.
body:
Thucydides' account of the war is the founding text of realist political analysis.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloponnesian_War).

name: Maya calendar systems
summary: The Maya ran interlocking cycles of 260 and 365 days alongside a Long Count that numbered every day from a fixed starting point.
body:
The 260-day tzolk'in and the 365-day haab' meshed in a 52-year round, while the Long Count counted days from a mythical zero point placed in 3114 BCE. Later Maya astronomers used the same arithmetic to tabulate the cycles of Venus and the seasons in which eclipses could fall.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_Long_Count_calendar).

name: Trial and death of Socrates
summary: Athens condemned Socrates to drink hemlock for impiety and corrupting the young.
body:
Through Plato and Aristotle his method of relentless questioning became the backbone of Western philosophy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Socrates).

name: Plato founds the Academy
summary: Plato opened a school in a grove outside Athens that taught mathematics, dialectic and philosophy and became a model for later institutions of learning.
body:
Plato taught that reality rests on abstract Forms reached through reason, and that geometry trained the mind to grasp them. The Academy taught until Sulla's sack of Athens in 86 BCE, was revived by later Platonists, and closed for good in 529 CE.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plato's_Academy).

name: Aristotle
summary: Aristotle systematised logic, biology, physics, ethics and politics, and tutored the young Alexander.
body:
His works dominated European and Islamic learning until the [Scientific Revolution](event:copernicus) began to overturn them.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle).

name: Conquests of Alexander the Great
summary: In eleven years Alexander destroyed the Persian Empire and led an army from Greece to the Punjab.
body:
He founded some twenty cities, [Alexandria](event:alexandria) chief among them, and after his death at 32 his generals carved the conquests into the Hellenistic kingdoms.

Greek language, art and civic forms spread from Egypt to Afghanistan and outlasted the empire that carried them there.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_Alexander_the_Great).

name: Battle of Gaugamela
summary: Alexander broke the main Persian army under Darius III, opening Mesopotamia and Persia to conquest.
body:
Part of [Conquests of Alexander the Great](event:alexander-conquests). Alexander broke the main Persian army under Darius III, opening Mesopotamia and Persia to conquest.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gaugamela).

name: Founding of Alexandria
summary: Alexander laid out a Greek city on the Egyptian coast that became the intellectual capital of the Mediterranean.
body:
Part of [Conquests of Alexander the Great](event:alexander-conquests). Its [Library and Museum](event:library-alexandria) drew scholars from across the Hellenistic world.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria).

name: Mauryan Empire and Ashoka
summary: Chandragupta Maurya unified most of the Indian subcontinent; his grandson Ashoka renounced war for Buddhism.
body:
After the bloodshed of the Kalinga campaign, Ashoka had edicts of tolerance and non-violence carved on rocks and pillars across his empire, and sent [Buddhist](event:buddha) missions as far as Sri Lanka and the Hellenistic kingdoms.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurya_Empire).

name: Roman road network expands
summary: Rome laid some 400,000 km of roads, about 80,000 km of them paved, transforming travel, trade and military logistics.
body:
Part of [Roman Republic formally established](event:roman-republic-founded). The Appian Way, begun in 312 BCE, set the standard: straight where possible, cambered for drainage, surfaced with fitted stone. A legion could march 30 km a day along them, and goods and messages moved across the empire in weeks rather than months.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_roads).

name: Epicureanism emerges
summary: Epicurus taught that pleasure — defined as absence of pain — is the good, and that simple life brings more pleasure than excess.
body:
Epicureanism was misunderstood in later ages as hedonism, but Epicurus himself lived plainly and advocated friendship, philosophy and modest food over luxury. His garden school in Athens became a lasting model of intellectual community.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epicureanism).

name: Meroitic script emerges
summary: The Kingdom of Kush developed its own alphabetic script to write the Meroitic language instead of Egyptian.
body:
Part of [Kingdom of Kush](event:nubian-kush). Meroitic has hieroglyphic and cursive forms and is read right to left. The signs can be sounded out, but the language behind them is still barely understood, so much of what the inscriptions say remains closed to us.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meroitic_script).

name: Roman concrete development
summary: Romans mixed lime, volcanic ash and seawater into a durable material that hardened underwater.
body:
Roman concrete (opus caementicium) let builders raise vaults, domes and harbour works far beyond what cut stone allowed. The Pantheon and the aqueducts depend on it, and its marine version, which sets under seawater, survives in harbours two thousand years on and is still studied by materials scientists.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_concrete).

name: Stoic philosophy founded
summary: Zeno of Citium taught that virtue is the highest good and that passion should be controlled by reason.
body:
Stoicism attracted Romans looking for an ethical framework: duty, reason, and apatheia — freedom from destructive passion. [Marcus Aurelius](event:marcus-aurelius), Seneca and the freed slave Epictetus became its best-known voices.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoicism).

name: Library of Alexandria
summary: The Ptolemies assembled the greatest collection of scrolls in the ancient world and paid scholars to work on them.
body:
Part of [Founding of Alexandria](event:alexandria). Eratosthenes measured the circumference of the Earth here to within a few percent; Euclid, Archimedes and Ptolemy all worked in its orbit. The library declined over centuries rather than perishing in a single fire.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Alexandria).

name: Punic Wars
summary: Three wars between Rome and Carthage decided who would rule the western Mediterranean.
body:
Hannibal crossed the Alps and destroyed Roman armies at [Cannae](event:cannae), but Rome outlasted him; [Scipio](event:zama) won at Zama, and in 146 BCE Carthage was razed and its territory annexed.

Victory turned Rome from an Italian power into a Mediterranean empire — and, in the process, strained the [Republic](event:roman-republic-fall) that had won it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars).

name: Qin unification of China
summary: Ying Zheng conquered the warring states and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of a unified China.
body:
He standardised script, coinage, weights and axle widths, linked frontier walls into an early [Great Wall](event:great-wall), and was buried with the [Terracotta Army](event:terracotta-army). The dynasty lasted fifteen years; the unified state it created has recurred ever since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_dynasty).

name: Great Wall of China
summary: Frontier walls were linked and repeatedly rebuilt over eighteen centuries; most of what survives is Ming work.
body:
Part of [Qin unification of China](event:qin-unification). Frontier walls were linked and repeatedly rebuilt over eighteen centuries; most of what survives is Ming work.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China).

name: Battle of Cannae
summary: Hannibal's double envelopment annihilated a much larger Roman army — still studied in military academies.
body:
Part of [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars). Hannibal's double envelopment annihilated a much larger Roman army — still studied in military academies.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae).

name: Terracotta Army
summary: Some 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers were buried to guard the first emperor's tomb; farmers rediscovered them in 1974.
body:
Part of [Qin unification of China](event:qin-unification). Some 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers were buried to guard the first emperor's tomb; farmers rediscovered them in 1974.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army).

name: Han dynasty
summary: Four centuries of Han rule set the pattern of Chinese imperial government and gave the majority ethnic group its name.
body:
The Han institutionalised [Confucian](event:confucius) learning in its bureaucracy, opened the [Silk Road](event:silk-road), and invented paper, the seismoscope and the wheelbarrow.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty).

name: Battle of Zama
summary: Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal in North Africa, ending the Second Punic War.
body:
Part of [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars). Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal in North Africa, ending the Second Punic War.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama).

name: Silk Road trade network
summary: Caravan routes linked China, Central Asia, Persia, India and the Mediterranean for some fifteen centuries.
body:
Silk, spices, paper, gunpowder, religions and — devastatingly — the [Black Death](event:black-death) all travelled these roads. The Han envoy Zhang Qian's mission west is the conventional starting point.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road).

name: Buddhism spreads along the Silk Road
summary: Buddhist monks and merchants carried the faith from India across Central Asia and into China.
body:
Part of [Life of the Buddha](event:buddha). Monks and merchants carried the teaching north into Bactria and along the [Silk Road](event:silk-road) oasis cities; it reached China by the first century CE. Monasteries became centres of translation and learning, and the religion adapted to each culture it entered.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism).

name: Nazca geoglyphs constructed
summary: The Nazca people of Peru scratched enormous geometric and animal figures into the desert floor.
body:
The lines stretch for miles — some outline spiders, hummingbirds and monkeys, others are long straight tracks and geometric figures. Their purpose is debated: astronomical markers, ritual pathways, or routes to water. Local people always knew of them, but their full shapes were only appreciated once aircraft flew over the pampa in the twentieth century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines).

name: Caesar's conquest of Gaul
summary: Eight years of campaigning brought Gaul under Roman rule and gave Caesar the army with which he seized power.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). Eight years of campaigning brought Gaul under Roman rule and gave Caesar the army with which he seized power.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallic_Wars).

name: Fall of the Roman Republic
summary: Civil war destroyed the republican constitution and left one man in charge of the Roman world.
body:
Caesar [crossed the Rubicon](event:rubicon) in 49 BCE, won the civil war, and was [assassinated](event:caesar-assassination) in 44. The wars that followed ended at [Actium](event:actium), leaving Octavian sole ruler and founding the [Empire](event:roman-empire).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Roman_Republic).

name: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
summary: Bringing a legion into Italy proper was an act of war against the Senate; Caesar did it anyway.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). Bringing a legion into Italy proper was an act of war against the Senate; Caesar did it anyway.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubicon).

name: Assassination of Julius Caesar
summary: Sixty senators stabbed the dictator to death at the Theatre of Pompey on the Ides of March, 44 BCE.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). The plot to save the Republic destroyed it: the resulting civil wars ended with Octavian as sole ruler.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Julius_Caesar).

name: Battle of Actium
summary: Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra off western Greece; Egypt was annexed the following year.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra off western Greece; Egypt was annexed the following year.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Actium).

name: Virgil composes the Aeneid
summary: Virgil's epic poem traced Rome's mythical origins and became the model of the heroic epic for two millennia.
body:
The Aeneid follows the Trojan Aeneas to Italy and ties Rome's origins to the settlement won under [Augustus](event:roman-empire). Written to stand beside Homer, it was read in schools for centuries as the benchmark of Latin verse.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid).

name: Founding of the Roman Empire
summary: The Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus and effective sole power, beginning two centuries of Roman peace.
body:
The *Pax Romana* united the Mediterranean under one law, one currency and a road network that would not be matched in Europe for well over a millennium.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire).

name: Ovid writes the Metamorphoses
summary: Ovid's epic poem narrated myths of transformation and became one of the most read works of the ancient world.
body:
The Metamorphoses connected mythical tales through the theme of change and rebirth. Written at the height of [the Augustan age](event:roman-empire), it's brimming with Ovid's wit and was hugely influential on medieval and Renaissance literature.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamorphoses).

name: Crucifixion of Jesus
summary: Jesus of Nazareth was executed in Roman Judaea; his followers' claim that he rose again founded Christianity.
body:
Within three centuries the movement had spread across the empire that killed him, and after [Constantine](event:constantine) it became the religion of the Roman state.

Christianity is today the largest religion in the world, and the Western calendar still counts from an estimate of his birth.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crucifixion_of_Jesus).

name: Colosseum construction in Rome
summary: The Flavian Amphitheatre was built under emperors Vespasian and Titus, the largest such structure in the ancient world.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). The Colosseum could seat 50,000 and was used for gladiatorial combats and public spectacles. It showcased the wealth, engineering and architectural ambition of the [Empire at its peak](event:rome-peak).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum).

links.label: Roman Empire at its greatest extent

name: Pliny the Elder's Natural History
summary: Pliny compiled an encyclopedic survey of everything known about the natural world, minerals, animals and plants.
body:
The Natural History gathers fact, folk belief and hearsay into thirty-seven books, and is our fullest window onto Roman knowledge of the natural world. Pliny died in 79 CE at Stabiae, having taken ships across the bay both to observe the [eruption of Vesuvius](event:vesuvius) and to take people off the shore.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_History_(Pliny)).

name: Eruption of Vesuvius destroys Pompeii
summary: A Plinian eruption buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under metres of ash and pyroclastic flow.
body:
Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay and left the first detailed description of a volcanic eruption. The buried towns preserve Roman daily life in unmatched detail — graffiti, bread, furniture and the voids left by the dead.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eruption_of_Mount_Vesuvius_in_79_AD).

name: Teotihuacan
summary: A city of over 100,000 people in the Valley of Mexico, laid out along the Avenue of the Dead.
body:
A city of over 100,000 people in the Valley of Mexico, laid out along the Avenue of the Dead.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan).

name: Moche civilisation of Peru
summary: The Moche of northern coastal Peru built irrigation canals, huge adobe platform mounds and the most expressive pottery in the Andes.
body:
Their modelled and painted vessels show hunting, warfare, ritual and everyday life in unusual detail. Moche engineers irrigated a desert coast from the river valleys, and their largest mound, the Huaca del Sol, is the biggest adobe structure in the Americas. The decline of the culture has been linked to prolonged drought and El Niño flooding.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moche_culture).

name: Rome supplied by eleven aqueducts
summary: By the early second century, eleven aqueducts carried roughly a million cubic metres of water a day into the city of Rome.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). Engineer Frontinus described the system in his treatise; water was distributed to public baths, fountains, sewers and some private homes. No other ancient city had such abundant fresh water or such sophisticated infrastructure.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqueduct_(Roman)).

name: Christianity spreads through the Roman Empire
summary: Three centuries after the crucifixion, Christianity had grown from a Judaean movement into a significant minority religion across the Mediterranean.
body:
Part of [Crucifixion of Jesus](event:crucifixion). Itinerant missionaries like Paul carried the faith along trade routes; communities worshipped in homes and catacombs despite periodic persecution. By 300 CE it had enough political weight to shape emperors.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Christianity).

name: Ancestral Puebloan civilization
summary: Ancestral Puebloans built cliff dwellings and vast trade networks in the American Southwest before abandoning the region around 1300.
body:
They left behind remarkable pueblos, kivas and thousands of petroglyphs. The reasons for their migration to river valleys remain debated — drought, social upheaval or resource depletion are all suggested.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancestral_Puebloans).

name: Paper invented in China
summary: Cai Lun reported to the court a method of making sheets from plant fibres, creating a revolution in writing.
body:
Part of [Han dynasty](event:han-dynasty). Paper was cheaper and lighter than silk or bamboo strips; it could be rolled into scrolls or folded into codices. It was kept secret in China for centuries, then spread westward along the [Silk Road](event:silk-road).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_paper).

name: Roman Empire at its greatest extent
summary: Under Trajan the empire reached from Britain to Mesopotamia, ruling perhaps a fifth of humanity.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). Under Trajan the empire reached from Britain to Mesopotamia, ruling perhaps a fifth of humanity.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan).

name: Pantheon completed in Rome
summary: Hadrian built the most complete Roman temple still standing, with a vast dome and oculus open to the sky.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). Its coffered dome, still the largest unreinforced concrete dome on Earth, opens to the sky through a nine-metre oculus, and the exterior was once clad in gilded bronze. Dedicated to the gods of Rome, it survived because it was later consecrated as a church.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome).

name: Marcus Aurelius and the Meditations
summary: The last of the Five Good Emperors wrote personal philosophical meditations on Stoicism while governing the empire.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). His writings, originally private journals, became a classic statement of duty, acceptance and virtue. Marcus Aurelius embodied the ideal of the philosopher-king.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius).

name: Antonine Plague
summary: An epidemic, probably smallpox, killed millions across the Roman world and thinned its armies.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). An epidemic, probably smallpox, killed millions across the Roman world and thinned its armies.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonine_Plague).

name: Classic Maya civilisation
summary: Maya city-states in the lowlands built stepped pyramids, tracked the planets and kept the most sophisticated writing system in the Americas.
body:
Their Long Count calendar recorded dates to the day across thousands of years. In the ninth century the southern cities were abandoned, probably under a combination of drought and warfare.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_civilization).

name: Kofun culture in Japan
summary: Japan's Kofun period saw the rise of a unified state, keyhole-shaped tombs, and early Chinese influence.
body:
Vast keyhole-shaped earthen tombs were raised for the elite, the largest covering more ground than any Egyptian pyramid. Bronze mirrors, iron armour and horse gear from the mounds show growing hierarchy and close contact with Korea. Chinese writing arrived during the period; Buddhism followed in the sixth century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofun_period).

name: Constantine legalises Christianity
summary: The Edict of Milan ended the persecution of Christians and set the empire on the path to a Christian state.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). Constantine also founded [Constantinople](event:constantinople-founded) and summoned the [Council of Nicaea](event:nicaea); by 380 Christianity was the official religion of Rome.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Milan).

name: Gupta Empire
summary: A classical age of Indian art, literature and mathematics under the Gupta kings.
body:
Aryabhata calculated pi and the length of the year; the [decimal place-value system](event:decimal-numerals) took its mature form in this period.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire).

name: First Council of Nicaea
summary: Bishops from across the empire agreed the Nicene Creed, defining orthodox Christian doctrine.
body:
Part of [Constantine legalises Christianity](event:constantine). Bishops from across the empire agreed the Nicene Creed, defining orthodox Christian doctrine.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Council_of_Nicaea).

name: Foundation of Constantinople
summary: Constantine refounded Byzantium as a new imperial capital that would outlast Rome itself by a thousand years.
body:
Part of [Constantine legalises Christianity](event:constantine). Constantine refounded Byzantium as a new imperial capital that would outlast Rome itself by a thousand years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople).

name: Migration Period
summary: Gothic, Vandal, Frankish and Hunnic peoples moved into the Roman provinces, remaking the map of Europe.
body:
The arrival of the Huns on the steppe set the movements going; within two centuries the western provinces had become Germanic kingdoms.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_Period).

name: Jerome translates the Bible into Latin
summary: Jerome produced the Vulgate, a Latin translation from Hebrew and Greek that became the Church's standard scripture for 1,200 years.
body:
Working mostly at Bethlehem, Jerome went back to the Hebrew for the Old Testament rather than relying on the Greek Septuagint. The Vulgate became the standard text of Latin Christendom, shaped the vocabulary of medieval Europe, and remained the Catholic Church's official Bible until modern scholarship produced new translations.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate).

name: Visigoths sack Rome
summary: Alaric's Goths took the city for the first time in eight hundred years, shocking the Roman world.
body:
Part of [Migration Period](event:migration-period). Alaric's Goths took the city for the first time in eight hundred years, shocking the Roman world.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410)).

name: Decimal place-value system and zero
summary: Indian mathematicians formalised positional decimal notation with zero as a number in its own right.
body:
Brahmagupta gave rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers in 628. Transmitted through [al-Khwarizmi](event:al-khwarizmi) to Europe, these numerals displaced Roman ones and made modern computation possible.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu–Arabic_numeral_system).

name: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
summary: The last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed at Ravenna, ending Roman rule in the west.
body:
The collapse was gradual — a century of [migrations](event:migration-period), civil wars and lost provinces, punctuated by the [sack of Rome](event:rome-sack-410) — but 476 remains the conventional date.

Western Europe fragmented into successor kingdoms, while the eastern half ruled from [Constantinople](event:constantinople-founded) continued for another thousand years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire).
